title: A Planted Forest and a Parade Ground: Harajuku and Yoyogi
standfirst: Two farming villages on a river terrace became the front approach to a shrine built entirely by human hand, and a shogunal drill field became, in turn, an aviation pioneers' runway, occupied family housing, an Olympic village and a park. Little of that sequence shows on the surface today, but the street plan still runs on it.

sections.heading: Two villages on a terrace above a stream

paragraphs.text: The land here is drier and higher than the river districts nearer the bay: the Geospatial Information Authority classes most of the study area as terrace and slope rather than flood plain, cut into by the small valley of a stream once called the Onden River. Before Edo grew this far, that terrace held two separate farming villages of Toshima District, Harajuku and Yoyogi, each recorded in an early nineteenth-century gazetteer with its own parish temple: Harajuku's Ryuganji kept a bell cast in 1762, Yoyogi's Fukusenji one cast in 1719. Onden, the third hamlet folded into this dossier's ground, took its name, an 1917 town survey records, from Onda Gorozaemon, a retainer of Uesugi Sadamasa who retired here and whose farming descendants gave the place its familiar name before the Tokugawa era respelled it with the characters now read Onden.

Under the shogunate the whole terrace was parcelled out to daimyo and hatamoto as detached residences and to temples as endowed land, the same 1917 survey notes: the Tokugawa main family's later estate had been the Kishu domain's own flower garden, the site of the Imperial Guard's 4th Regiment had belonged to a hatamoto named Mizuno, and the district still called Shin-yashiki, "new residence," took its name from land once held by Naito Tango-no-kami and later divided among his retainers. Harajuku's own name is explained two ways in the same source: either from a post-station on the old road from Kamakura to Mutsu province, or, in a tradition kept at Ryuganji, from the eleventh-century general Minamoto no Yoshiie mustering his troops here before an eastern campaign, a story the slope by the temple gate still marks as Seizoroizaka, "muster slope."

sections.heading: A parade ground for a modernising army

paragraphs.text: Meiji rule turned the largest open part of this terrace into a military exercise field, the Yoyogi Parade Ground, and for three decades it did service as much for spectacle and invention as for drill. Visiting royalty were reviewed there: a 1922 commemorative album of the Prince of Wales's state visit devotes two full plates to the military review staged for him at Yoyogi. More lastingly, it was here, on 19 December 1910, that the army officers Tokugawa Yoshitoshi and Hino Kumagoro made Japan's first officially recognised powered flights, an event the National Diet Library's own history of Japanese aviation still marks as the country's aviation centenary starting point: Tokugawa's Henri Farman biplane, bought in France, reached about 70 metres and 53 kilometres an hour over roughly three kilometres in a four-minute flight, after the two men had spent four months training in Europe that year.

By the 1910s the farming villages around the parade ground were filling with commuters. Harajuku, Onden and Sendagaya had merged into a single Sendagaya village in 1889, the 1917 town survey records, and its population grew sharply after the wars with China and Russia as Tokyo's middle class looked for houses within reach of the city; in 1907 the village became Sendagaya Town outright. A 1922 land-value survey of the town shows Harajuku itself already subdivided into named micro-districts such as North Harajuku and South Harajuku, evidence of how built-up the old village core had become even before its next transformation.

sections.heading: A shrine, and a forest built to outlast its builders

paragraphs.text: That transformation was Meiji Shrine. After Emperor Meiji's death in 1912 and Empress Shoken's in 1914, the Home Ministry set up a Meiji Shrine Construction Bureau in 1915, and the 1917 Sendagaya town survey, written while the work was still under way, already notes that the shrine's inner precinct was fixed on the Yoyogi imperial estate, its outer garden on the Aoyama parade ground, and that both the front approach and a back approach linking the two would run through the town, reason enough, its compilers felt, to record the shrine's coming specially even before it opened. The shrine was dedicated on 1 November 1920, and its outer garden, with the ginkgo avenue still associated with it, was finished in October 1926.

The forest around the inner shrine was not inherited but designed. Three forestry and landscape specialists, led by Honda Seiroku, surveyed some 88 shrine forests across Japan and, against the Home Minister's own preference for a conifer plantation on the Nikko model, argued for a broadleaf forest that would need almost no maintenance and would evolve through natural succession over fifty, a hundred and a hundred and fifty years. About 100,000 trees, donated from across the country, were set out over the roughly 70-hectare inner precinct by some 110,000 volunteer young people, an act of civic labour on a scale Tokyo had not seen before.

sections.heading: 1932: the ward that did not want to be born

paragraphs.text: Tokyo's expansion from 15 to 35 wards in 1932 required Sendagaya to give up the independence it had only gained in 1907, merging with Shibuya and Yoyohata towns on 1 October that year to form Shibuya Ward. Sendagaya, debt-free and home to the Tokugawa family's main residence, fought the merger hard, a Kokugakuin University account of the episode records: it had petitioned since 1930 to join the more established Yotsuya or Akasaka wards instead, proposed the alternative name Jingu-ku, "Shrine Ward," in deference to its new neighbour, and marked the merger date itself with banners reading "never forget the first of October," a day its residents called Ankoku De, "Dark Day." The new ward assembly, dominated by Shibuya and Yoyohata representatives, rejected the appeal, and the Sendagaya name survives today only as a district within Shibuya.

sections.heading: 1945: the shrine burns, the parade ground becomes a base

paragraphs.text: The shrine's own chronology records what the war did to it with unusual precision: on 14 April 1945, American B-29 bombers set its main hall and worship hall ablaze, forcing worship to stop for two days while its sacred objects were moved into the treasure house for safety. Reconstruction funds began arriving within days, and a temporary worship hall went up that same month, but the permanent rebuilding took over a decade; the rededication of the new main hall, attended by more than six thousand people including members of the imperial family, was finally held on 31 October 1958.

Across the old parade ground, the occupation of Japan left a longer mark. The former Yoyogi Parade Ground became Washington Heights, family housing for American service personnel, and it stayed under American control until Tokyo's own Olympic ambitions reclaimed it: for the 1964 Games it served as the main athletes' village, and one surviving cottage, once home to the Dutch team, still stands in what is now Yoyogi Park. Beside it, on part of the same reclaimed ground, Kenzo Tange's National Yoyogi Stadium, built for the Games' swimming and basketball events and completed in September 1964, used a then-unprecedented cable suspension roof that a workforce of some 200,000 built in eighteen months, a construction feat covered on national television as it happened.

Meiji Shrine's forest, still developing broadly as its Taisho-era planners predicted, remains the largest single feature on the map, and Omotesando, opened as the shrine's formal approach in 1920, still runs dead straight toward it from Aoyama-dori. West of the shrine, the old Onden River survives only as a route: it was culverted and its bed became a footpath that Shibuya Ward has since officially named Cat Street, continuing south past Omotesando as the Former Shibuya River Promenade, with old bridge-post markers still standing along the way to show where it once ran in the open.

Yoyogi Park's slightly irregular paths and open lawns, unusual for a Japanese metropolitan park, are themselves a trace of its double reuse: first as barrack housing laid out on the old parade ground's grid, then as an Olympic village whose surviving buildings and street pattern still shape the park built over them after 1964. Between the shrine's dense forest and the park's open ground, the terrace-and-slope landform recorded for this district by the land-survey authority is easiest to feel on foot, in the short, sharp drop from Sendagaya's old high ground down toward the former streambed that Cat Street now follows.

timeline.what: Bell-casting dates recorded for Harajuku village's Ryuganji and Yoyogi village's Fukusenji, evidence both existed as separate Edo-period villages.
Harajuku, Onden and Sendagaya villages merge into a single Sendagaya village.
Tokugawa Yoshitoshi and Hino Kumagoro make Japan's first officially recognised powered flights at Yoyogi Parade Ground.
Sendagaya village becomes Sendagaya Town as Tokyo's commuter suburbs expand.
The Meiji Shrine Construction Bureau is established after the deaths of Emperor Meiji (1912) and Empress Shoken (1914).
Meiji Shrine is dedicated; its front approach, Omotesando, opens the same year.
Meiji Shrine's outer garden is completed.
Sendagaya, Shibuya and Yoyohata towns merge into Shibuya Ward, against fierce Sendagaya resistance.
American B-29 bombing burns Meiji Shrine's main hall and worship hall.
Meiji Shrine's rebuilt main hall is rededicated.
The former Washington Heights site serves as the Tokyo Olympics' athletes' village; the National Yoyogi Stadium is completed in September.
The former parade-ground and Olympic-village site opens as Yoyogi Park.

walk.name: Omotesando
walk.what: Meiji Shrine's formal approach, laid out from Aoyama-dori to the shrine and opened in 1920 alongside the shrine itself, still runs on its original straight line.

walk.name: Meiji Shrine forest and main hall
walk.what: A deliberately designed broadleaf forest planted from 1915 by some 110,000 volunteers; the main hall was rebuilt after the 1945 firebombing and rededicated in 1958.

walk.name: Cat Street
walk.ja: キャットストリート（旧渋谷川遊歩道路）
walk.what: A ward-designated footpath following the culverted course of the old Onden/Shibuya River south past Omotesando; old bridge-post markers survive along the route.

walk.name: Yoyogi Park
walk.what: Former Yoyogi Parade Ground, then the postwar Washington Heights family-housing site, then the 1964 Olympic athletes' village; a surviving cottage once housing the Dutch team still stands near the park entrance.

walk.name: National Yoyogi Stadium
walk.what: Kenzo Tange's cable-suspension-roofed arena, built on part of the same former parade ground for the 1964 Olympics' swimming and basketball events, completed that September.

walk.name: Takeshita-dori
walk.what: Runs through the old core of Harajuku village, subdivided into named micro-districts such as North and South Harajuku by the time of a 1922 land-value survey.

caveats: Yoyogi Park's exact opening year (1967) is corroborated only through search summaries of official Tokyo Metropolitan Government planning documents this session, not by reading an official page's full text directly; the wider sequence (parade ground, Washington Heights, Olympic village, park) is independently confirmed by the park authority's own page.

The Onden/Shibuya River's exact culverting date is not given by any source read this session; it is described here only as having happened by the postwar decades, since only the river's present course and official path name could be verified.

Village- and shrine-name etymologies (Harajuku, Onden, Sendagaya) are given as recorded in a 1917 town survey and an 1826-derived gazetteer compilation, which themselves note some traditions as oral or uncertain.

Meiji Shrine's own founding traditions and the exact wartime casualty picture for Sendagaya's air raids were outside what this session could verify from primary sources; only the shrine's own building-history chronology is used for 1945 and 1958.
